content: Redness in the eye occurs due to swelling or dilation of blood vessels, which makes the surface of the eye appear red or bloodshot. There are numerous potential causes for red eyes, ranging from benign conditions to serious medical emergencies. The degree of redness is often less concerning than the presence of associated symptoms such as pain or visual disturbances. Causes of Red Eye: 1. Swollen Blood Vessels in the Sclera: The redness is caused by the swelling of blood vessels in the white part of the eye (sclera). This can result from environmental factors such as dry air, excessive sun exposure, dust, or the presence of a foreign object in the eye. Allergies, infections, or trauma can also contribute. 2. Subconjunctival Hemorrhage: Straining or coughing can lead to a bright red, dense bloody area on the sclera, known as a subconjunctival hemorrhage. While alarming in appearance, this condition is common and typically harmless. If you notice a painless bloody spot in one eye, it usually resolves on its own within one to two weeks. 3. Eye Infections or Inflammation: These conditions can cause redness along with symptoms such as itching, discharge, pain, or vision problems. Examples include: Blepharitis: Inflammation of the eyelash margins along the edge of the eyelid. Conjunctivitis (Pink Eye): Swelling or infection of the conjunctiva, the tissue lining the eyelids and covering the eye's surface. Corneal Ulcers: Open sores on the cornea, often due to bacterial or viral infections. Uveitis: Inflammation of the uvea, which includes the iris, ciliary body, and choroid. This condition is often linked to autoimmune disorders, infections, or toxin exposure. When only the iris is inflamed, it is referred to as iritis. 4. Other Causes: Common colds or allergies. Acute Glaucoma: A sudden increase in intraocular pressure, causing severe pain and significant visual disturbances. This is a medical emergency. Corneal scratches from sand, dust, or prolonged contact lens use. Diagnosis: A healthcare provider will perform a physical examination, including an eye exam, and inquire about your medical history. Questions may include: Are one or both eyes affected? If only one, which one? What part of the eye is red—the sclera or another area? Did the redness appear suddenly? Have you experienced eye redness before? Are you experiencing eye pain? Does it worsen with eye movement? Are there other symptoms such as discharge, burning, itching, nausea, vomiting, or headache? When to Seek Urgent Medical Care: Seek immediate medical attention or call emergency services if: The redness follows a penetrating eye injury. You experience a headache along with blurred vision or confusion. You see halos around lights. You have nausea and vomiting. Contact your healthcare provider if: Redness persists for more than 1–2 days. You experience eye pain or changes in vision. You are on blood-thinning medications like warfarin. You suspect a foreign object in your eye. You are highly sensitive to light. You notice yellow or greenish discharge from one or both eyes. Treatment Options: For eye strain or fatigue, resting the eyes is often sufficient, and no specific treatment is required. However, if you experience pain or vision problems, consult a healthcare provider. Treatment may involve rinsing the eyes with saline solution, removing any foreign objects, or prescribing eye drops.
